Anthony Museum & House Expansion Rochester Gas Prices Pet of the Week Do The Right Thing ESL Heart of Service Award Careers × Watch Now: News10NBC at 7 County health officials warn about possible measles exposure at Strong’s emergency department Evan Bourtis, Adelisa Badžić News10NBC Updated: September 10, 2026 - 1:06 AM Published: September 9, 2026 - 1:18 PM Measles graphic (file image) ROCHESTER, N.Y. — A person with measles visited Strong Memorial Hospital’s emergency department earlier this month, potentially exposing about 100 people to the highly contagious virus. The infected person, who was not vaccinated and is not a Monroe County resident, was in the adult or pediatric emergency departments from 11 p.m. on Sept. 7 through 2 a.m. on Sept. 8, Monroe County health officials Wednesday. RELATED: More measles cases confirmed in Steuben County, health official weighs in on staying safe “Measles is a highly contagious respiratory disease, so it’s caused by a virus that spread by direct contact with either nasal secretions or from the throat,” said Dr. Marielena Vélez de Brown, the county’s commissioner for public health. “It is such a small virus that it can hang out in the air in a space for two hours after a patient has left.” The Monroe County Department of Public Health is reviewing records of patients who were in the emergency department during the exposure period. Hospital or county health officials will contact anyone who was there without documented evidence of immunity. Anyone who was in the emergency department during that time should monitor themselves for symptoms through Sept. 28. The department’s phone number is 585-753-5555. “If you start to feel ill, do not go straight into the doctors,” Dr. Vélez de Brown said. “This is the one time when I would ask, definitely contact your healthcare provider or call the emergency department, but let them know the concern that you were potentially in one of these two locations in recent weeks where we’ve had exposures.” Tracking measles cases locally Measles is a very contagious respiratory disease, caused by a virus and spread by contact with nasal or throat secretions of infected people. The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in 35 years, and News10NBC has been tracking cases locally. Here are the latest numbers: At least 10 confirmed cases in Steuben County At least five confirmed cases in Seneca County At least two confirmed cases in Ontario County At least one confirmed case in Yates County In addition, a person infected with measles traveled through the Louise M. Slaughter Train Station in Rochester on Saturday, Aug. 29. Monroe County health officials say the person wasn’t a county resident, but may have exposed others. The risk of getting measles is low for people who have gotten vaccinated or have had measles in the past. You can learn more about getting vaccinated here. Symptoms of measles Measles symptoms usually appear 10 to 12 days after exposure but may take as long as 21 days. Symptoms typically appear in two stages. The first stage includes a runny nose, cough, and a slight fever. In addition, eyes may become reddened and small bluish-white spots, surrounded by a red area, may appear in the mouth. The second stage includes a red blotchy rash lasting five to six days. The rash usually begins on the face and then spreads downward and outward, reaching the hands and feet. If you have measles symptoms, call your doctor before going to a clinic, so they can prevent you from exposing others. “The best way that the community can protect itself is by vaccination,” Dr. Vélez de Brown said. “One MMR vaccine is calculated to be 93% effective in preventing a person from developing measles if they have been exposed. And then the combination of two valid MMR vaccines is up to 97% effective.” Monroe County’s vaccination rate is 86% of children having had one dose by two years of age, down from 87% in January 2025. Health officials recommend children receive the MMR vaccine at their first birthday and fourth birthday. For families traveling, officials recommend children can receive the MMR vaccine as early as six months of age, though this does not replace the need for vaccines at one year and four years. “We are seeing vaccine rates dropping across the country,” Dr. Vélez de Brown added. “Even here, amongst a very well-educated, well-informed population, we’re seeing the trend of slowly decreasing rates of folks being vaccinated.” Again, anyone with concerns about potential exposure can call the Monroe County Department of Public Health at 585-753-5555. Residents of other counties should contact their local health departments. MessageFacebookMessengerRedditWhatsAppCopy LinkEmailXShare ✓ Thanks for sharing! More

Public Health Coroner Confirms Measles Killed Pennsylvania Infant As Federal Count Still Lags Federal health officials have not added either of the two infant deaths reported last month to national totals You can still access 2 more articles for free. - A Pennsylvania coroner says measles killed one of two infants who died in the state last month - The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has not yet counted either death in national totals - Pennsylvania's measles outbreak has grown to more than 620 cases across 37 counties this year THURSDAY, Sept. 10, 2026 (HealthDay News) — A Pennsylvania coroner has confirmed that measles killed one of two infants who died in the state last month, but federal health officials still are not counting either death in the national measles tally. Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, said Wednesday that he has shared his conclusions with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Associated Press reports. Mary Stoltzfus was 6 weeks old when she died at home Aug. 18. She was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare inherited condition that causes an unusually small head and an underdeveloped brain. Children born with it typically live six months or less. The condition left her with very little defense against infection, and a measles infection killed her, Diamantoni told AP News. His office did not perform an autopsy on the girl. Her cause of death was determined by the doctors treating her. Ivan Miller died Aug. 14, shortly after he was born, of a ruptured spleen. Diamantoni's office did perform an autopsy on the boy, he said. Exactly how and when the spleen ruptured is still under investigation. The boy was infected with measles, and the virus is listed on his death certificate as a contributing factor. But Diamantoni said measles played no role in the spleen injury and is noted only because it was a significant condition the boy had when he died. The first dose of measles vaccine is usually given around age 1, meaning neither infant was old enough to receive it for protection from the virus's spread. The CDC's measles webpage briefly listed two measles-associated deaths, then was changed to say the agency would not count them until it reviewed more information. The page, last updated Friday, still does not reflect either death. The deaths also set off a public clash between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat who said vaccination could have prevented them, and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who suggested the deaths might have been made up, reports AP News. Kennedy has a long history of vaccine skepticism. Both deaths are documented in official records, including an autopsy in one case, and Kennedy acknowledged the coroner's measles finding in a social media post last week. The dispute has left some public health leaders uneasy about federal data. "Frankly, the CDC is not to be trusted in sharing information," Dr. Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association, told AP News. He said people are questioning the agency's motives. Meanwhile, the state's outbreak keeps growing. As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania had recorded more than 620 measles cases in 37 counties this year, state officials said. The U.S. once halted the routine spread of measles within its borders. However, vaccination rates have since slipped below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. International health officials plan to meet in November to decide whether the United States has lost its measles-free status. More information Visit the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for more information about measles vaccination. SOURCE: AP News, Sept. 9, 2026 Babies younger than 1 year are too young for the measles vaccine, so their protection depends on the people around them. People should make sure everyone in their household is up to date on their shots. www.healthday.com

Health officials in Kane County also confirmed a second measles case for the area. By Sun-Times Wire Sept 10, 2026, 6:44pm UTC The Chicago Department of Public Health warned of a potential measles exposure at Union Station in August. Kane County health officials also confirmed its second case of measles. AP file SHARE COPY LINK Share CLOSE Twitter Facebook Bluesky Email Reddit Flipboard An out-of-state domestic traveler with a confirmed case of measles passed through Union Station in the West Loop late last month, Chicago health authorities announced Thursday. The stricken traveler was at Union Station in the 200 block of South Canal Street on Thursday, Aug. 27th after 8:00 p.m. through Friday, Aug. 28th, according to a statement from the Chicago Department of Public Health. CDPH didn’t provide a time for the traveler’s departure. The exact date and time of exposure are unknown at this time. If more information becomes available, CDPH will update the exposure location posting on its website. A second measles case was also confirmed in Kane County Thursday, weeks after the area’s first confirmed case, according to health officials. The person was vaccinated against measles and in contact with the first case, which was first reported Aug. 24, according to the Kane County Health Department. While a vaccination protects against measles, breakthrough cases, where a vaccinated person can get measles, still occur, health officials said. People who are vaccinated and develop measles are generally less likely to experience severe illness or complications and may be less likely to transmit the virus. The first confirmed case in Kane County included two possible exposure locations: Kaneland High School in Maple Park on Aug. 18, during the school day. Next Generation Pediatric Clinic in South Elgin on Aug, 21, between 12:30 p.m. and 4 p.m. As of Thursday, there were 11 reported measles cases in the state, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. supplementary_news.content: FOX 2 Possible measles exposure reported at Missouri train station Alex Barton 2 days ago JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. — Missouri health officials are warning of a possible measles exposure at the Sedalia train station after a Missouri resident confirmed to have the virus got on a train headed to Chicago on Aug. 27. According to the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the person boarded Amtrak Train 318 at the Sedalia station while going through Pettis County to another destination. The person is not a resident of Pettis County. Officials said details about the possible exposure are limited at this time. More information will be provided if it becomes available. People who may have been exposed should monitor themselves for measles symptoms for three weeks after the exposure date and contact their local public health agency if symptoms develop. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness. One person with measles can spread it to as many as nine out of 10 people near them who are unvaccinated or don’t have natural immunity, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Symptoms usually consist of fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. A rash typically pops up three to five days after the initial symptoms and usually starts on the face near the hairline before spreading down the body. The virus can spread through direct contact or through the air when a person who’s infected breathes, coughs, or sneezes. It can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area, DHSS says. People who think they might have measles should isolate themselves, then call their healthcare provider before going to a doctor’s office. Patients should tell their provider they are concerned about measles and follow instructions for getting tested and treated without exposing other people. Measles can cause serious complications like pneumonia and encephalitis, and can be deadly. The best way to prevent measles is vaccination. Two doses of a measles vaccine gives about 97% protection against the infection. The CDC and Missouri DHSS recommend kids get their first dose at 12 to 15 months old and a second dose at 4 to 6 years old. Unvaccinated adults can also get a catch-up MMR vaccine. Measles can be especially dangerous for pregnant women, their unborn children, and babies who are too young to be vaccinated. More information about measles and MMR vaccination rates is available through the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. Ad Your Privacy Choices

New River Valley Christiansburg ups requirements for any future data center There will be no by-right use in the town without provisions. A special thanks to our Cornerstone Partners Organizations who give $10K or more per year Sports With appeals rulings, VHSL realignment is complete. Here’s who’s moving and who’s staying. The Virginia High School League has ruled on appeals stemming from its recent realignment plan.
